title: The CEO Has No KPI
author: Managing the Future
summary: Responding to a viral 'Top 18 KPIs for CEOs' graphic, the author argues that every metric on such lists already belongs to a functional executive (sales, marketing, finance, product, people, or customer), and that a CEO who personally manages any of them is doing their team's job instead of their own. When a CEO adopts a favorite functional KPI as their personal target, it distorts the whole company: chasing revenue growth, for instance, can starve product investment and drive up churn eighteen months later. The real job of a CEO, the piece argues, is integrating across all six functional areas under uncertainty, resolving tradeoffs no single functional executive is positioned to see, using an extended metaphor of six wheels on a vehicle that the CEO must keep turning in a coordinated way.
points: Every metric on a typical 'CEO KPI' list (CAC, churn, EBITDA, NPS, etc.) actually belongs to a specific functional executive, not the CEO.
A CEO who personally manages functional KPIs like revenue or churn is doing the work of their executive team and abdicating their real job.
Optimizing for one favorite metric (e.g., revenue growth) can quietly destabilize the whole system — margin erodes, churn rises later, and product investment dries up.
The CEO's actual job is multivariable optimization under uncertainty: resolving tradeoffs across functions that no single functional executive can see.
Analogy: the six functional areas of a business are like six wheels on a vehicle; the CEO's job is to notice which wheel is turning slowest, since that's what constrains the whole machine.
quotes: none of these are “KPIs for the CEO.” I know that sounds a little pedantic, but to position these items as “for the CEO” misunderstands what the CEO job actually is.
Not one of the 18 KPIs measures the business as a whole. They measure the performance of a function within the business.
By optimizing one variable, the CEO has destabilized the whole system.
The job is multivariable optimization under uncertainty, i.e., the hardest kind of work there is.
the six areas of the business are like six wheels on a vehicle. The CEO's job is to make sure all six wheels are turning in a coordinated way
